newsitem.title: GERMANY: Issing urges early fixes of forex rates before EMU.
newsitem.headline: Issing urges early fixes of forex rates before EMU.

text.p: A senior member of Germany's Bundesbank on Saturday called for an early decision to be made on fixing exchange rates for countries joining European monetary union (EMU).

Chief economist Otmar Issing told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung newspaper that exchange rates should be pegged when the decision is taken early next year on which countries will form EMU's starting lineup in 1999.

"I think it would be sensible that when the participating countries are chosen early next year, the conversion rates are also fixed," Issing, who is also a member of the Bundesbank council, told the newspaper.
Issing added that fixing the exchange rates at which countries would give up their currencies in favour of the euro would also create "certainty of expectations in the markets".
"Speculation against a credible decision would then be suicide," Issing told the newspaper.

Issing also said there should be no surprises in deciding which countries join EMU. Countries carrying out accounting tricks or one-off measures to meet the Maastricht treaty convergence criteria should not be admitted.

Countries seeking to join the single currency project are required under the Maastricht criteria to meet tough borrowing targets, but the treaty only sets January 1, 1999 as a final date for fixing exchange rates irrevocably.

Issing also said it would be a mistake to think that the Bundesbank would give up its freedom to adjust German interest rates as it viewed appropriate in the runup to EMU -- even if exchange rates were pegged.
"It would be wrong simply to think that nothing can change on interest rates," Issing said.
And, if the Bundesbank decided to raise interest rates, that would not be a hostile act against the rest of Europe, he said.

"The basic view that an increase in interest rates would be hostile towards Europe just doesn't stand up. If a rate rise is needed to defend the stability of the currency, then it is not just in the national, but in the European interest," he said.

If currency rates are fixed next year, then coordination would be needed which would usher in the type of cooperation that would prevail when the European Central Bank takes over the running of monetary policy after EMU, he said.
"The actions of the central banks would have to go in the same direction, what matters is the common interest in stability," Issing said.
